                                   ECE2.414 · Advanced Memory Circuits and Systems


                                           Assignment 1
                              Simulating Memory: Devices to Systems
                                     ngspice · CACTI · NVSim · Ramulator · gem5
                                    Priyesh Shukla · IIIT Hyderabad · Monsoon 2026



Overview
This assignment carries one design question through five simulation tools, each operating at a different level of
abstraction. The central question is:
                    "Should the 2 MB L2 cache in our accelerator be SRAM, or STT-MRAM?"
Each part answers one question that none of the other four tools can. The output of each part is a number you
carry into the next part's input file. Report ratios between configurations, not absolute numbers — ratios survive
the compounding errors.
  Submission: One PDF, 6-8 pages — five tables, four plots, and the two-paragraph argument from Part E Task
  4. Working in pairs is encouraged.
Marking: 20 % Part E argument · 60 % remaining questions · 20 % report & reproducible codes (provide GitHub repo link in
report)


  Part A — ngspice: Read a 6T SRAM cell and measure the margin


Central question — Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7 V and 85 °C?
  Use the netlist below (45 nm PTM BSIM4, Q = 0, QB = 1 stored). The cell ratio is deliberately marginal — Task 2
  is meant to fail.
  * AMCAS TakeHomeLab - 6T read, bitline discharge and margin
  .include 45nm_bulk.txt        $ PTM BSIM4 card
  .param VDD=1.1 VBL=1.1
  Vdd vdd 0 'VDD'
  Vwl wl 0 PWL(0 0 1n 0 1.05n 'VDD')
  MP1 qb q vdd vdd pmos W=0.15u L=0.045u
  MN1 qb q 0     0   nmos W=0.20u L=0.045u
  MP2 q qb vdd vdd pmos W=0.15u L=0.045u
  MN2 q qb 0     0   nmos W=0.20u L=0.045u
  MA1 bl wl q 0      nmos W=0.16u L=0.045u
  MA2 blb wl qb 0    nmos W=0.16u L=0.045u
  Cbl bl 0 180f IC='VBL'
  Cblb blb 0 180f IC='VBL'
  .ic v(q)=0 v(qb)='VDD'
  .control
    tran 5p 4n uic
    meas tran dv   FIND v(blb)-v(bl) AT=2.0n
    meas tran qmax MAX v(q) FROM=1n TO=4n
    wrdata read.csv v(bl) v(blb) v(q) v(qb)
  .endc
  .end



  Task 1. Report ΔV(BL,BLB) at t = 2 ns. Compare it with the 69 mV reference value given in Lecture 1.
  Task 2. Plot v(q). Does it move during the read? Grow MA1 and MA2 to W = 0.24 µm and re-run — what
  happens now? [deliberately marginal; expect a failure]
  Task 3. Sweep V_DD from 1.1 V down to 0.6 V in 50 mV steps using a .control loop. Plot ΔV vs V_DD and find
  the voltage at which ΔV falls below the 25 mV sense-amp offset from Lecture 5.
  Task 4. Repeat Task 1 at .temp 85. In one paragraph state which of ΔV and the sense-amp offset moved more,
  and which one sets the failure.

  ⚠ Note: ngspice is the only tool in this assignment that solves physics. Everything above it solves arithmetic. Your CACTI
  numbers in Part B are curve-fits to results like these.




 Part B — CACTI: Size the 2 MB SRAM L2


Central question — How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45 nm?
 CACTI does not simulate a single transistor. It performs an exhaustive search over array organisations (Ndwl ×
 Ndbl × Nspd for data; Ntwl × Ntbl × Ntspd for tags) and scores each candidate with analytical delay, energy, and
 area models, then returns the organisation that minimises your objective.
  # cache.cfg (CACTI 7)
  -size (bytes) 2097152
  -block size (bytes) 64
  -associativity 8
  -read-write port 1
  -UCA bank count 4
  -technology (u) 0.045
  -operating temperature (K) 350
  -cache type "cache"
  -Data array cell type - "itrs-hp"
  -Data array peripheral type - "itrs-hp"
  -Optimize ED or ED^2 (ED, ED^2, NONE): "ED^2"
  -design objective (weight delay, dynamic power,
   leakage power, cycle time, area) 0:0:0:100:0

  $ ./cacti -infile cache.cfg



 Task 1. Run CACTI. Record access time (ns), dynamic read energy (pJ), leakage (mW), and area (mm²). This is
 your SRAM baseline for Parts C, D, and E.
 Task 2. Sweep capacity from 256 kB to 16 MB (everything else fixed). Plot access time against log₂(capacity). Is
 Amrutur & Horowitz's "one gate delay per doubling" visible?
 Task 3. Change only the objective — run once for pure delay, once for pure area, once for ED²P. Report the
 three winning Ndwl/Ndbl triples and explain why the optimal organisation changes.
 Task 4. Take CACTI's bitline delay for your Task 1 winner and hand-check it against 0.38 · R · C · L² from Lecture
 4. Report the discrepancy and name one effect CACTI models that your hand calculation does not.
  ⚠ Note: Task 3 is the one that matters. There is no such thing as 'the optimal cache' — only the optimum of the
  objective you wrote down.




 Part C — NVSim: The same 2 MB as STT-MRAM


Central question — Same capacity, same periphery — different bitcell. What changes?
 NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted into a separate text file you supply. The array organisation,
 peripheral search, and output format are identical. Your results are exactly as good as the .cell file you feed it.
  # sample.cell (STT-MRAM, 16 lines)
  -MemCellType: MRAM
  -CellArea (F^2): 54
  -CellAspectRatio: 2.0
  -ResistanceOn (ohm): 3000
  -ResistanceOff (ohm): 6000
  -ReadMode: current
  -ReadCurrent (uA): 40
  -ReadPower (uW): 145
  -ResetMode: current
  -ResetCurrent (uA): 200
  -ResetPulse (ns): 10
  -SetMode: current

  -SetCurrent (uA): 200
  -SetPulse (ns): 10
  -AccessType: CMOS
  -AccessCMOSWidth (F): 6

  $ ./nvsim ./config/STT_cache.cfg



 Task 1. Run NVSim at 2 MB with the shipped STT-MRAM cell. Tabulate read latency, write latency, read energy,
 write energy, leakage, and area side-by-side with your CACTI SRAM baseline from Part B.
 Task 2. Two of those six metrics will be dramatically worse and two dramatically better. Identify which ones
 and explain the difference in device terms — not 'because the tool said so'.
 Task 3. The TMR ratio here is 2:1 (3 kΩ / 6 kΩ). Re-run with R_on = 4 kΩ and R_off = 12 kΩ. Which output
 metric moved most? Explain what a device paper's TMR headline actually buys at the array level.
 Task 4. Halve ResetCurrent to 100 µA and re-run. Note what happened to area and explain the mechanism —
 this is the single most important coupling in NVM array design.
  ⚠ Note: Task 4: write current → sizes the access transistor → sets cell area → sets the density advantage you bought the
  technology for. Follow that chain explicitly in your write-up.




 Part D — Ramulator 2.0: L2 miss stream on a DDR4 channel


Central question — Does the changed miss traffic still fit in one DDR4 channel?
 A DRAM simulator contains no charge, no capacitor, and no sense amplifier. It is a table of timing constraints
 (tRCD, tRP, tRAS, tCCD), a state machine per bank, and a scheduler that issues the next legal command.
 Generate the trace from gem5's CommMonitor on your L2's memory-side port.
  # ddr4.yaml (Ramulator 2.0)
  Frontend:
    impl: SimpleO3
    traces: [ l2miss.trace ]
    clock_ratio: 8
  MemorySystem:
    impl: GenericDRAM
    clock_ratio: 3
    DRAM:
      impl: DDR4
      org: { preset: DDR4_8Gb_x8, channel: 1, rank: 2 }
      timing: { preset: DDR4_3200AA }
    Controller:
      impl: Generic
      Scheduler: { impl: FRFCFS }
      RefreshManager: { impl: AllBank }
      plugins: [ { ControllerPlugin: { impl: TraceRecorder } } ]

  # l2miss.trace      (one access per line)
  0x7f2a4c00 R
  0x7f2a4c40 R
  0x7f2a5000 W

  $ ./ramulator2 -f ddr4.yaml



 Task 1. Run Ramulator. Report memory_cycles, total read/write latency, and the row-buffer hit rate from the
 stats dump.
 Task 2. Switch Scheduler from FRFCFS to FCFS. Row-buffer hit rate will collapse. Quantify the latency cost in
 cycles and explain it in terms of tRCD and tRP.
 Task 3. Change the address mapping so the row bits sit below the bank bits. Re-run. Quantify the loss of bank-
 level parallelism.
 Task 4. Double the channel count. If latency barely improves, identify which of the four DRAM timing
 parameters is binding and explain how you would determine this from the output.

  ⚠ Note: Generate l2miss.trace yourself: the CommMonitor on gem5's L2 memory-side port produces exactly this format.




  Part E — gem5: Run the whole thing


Central question — Does the program you actually care about run faster?
  gem5 is the only tool in this assignment that can answer the central question in cycles. The L2 hit latency you
  pass to gem5 comes from CACTI and NVSim; the capacity trade comes from their area outputs. gem5 invents
  neither. Warm up atomically for tens of millions of accesses before switching to O3CPU.
  # Baseline — CACTI SRAM L2
  $ build/X86/gem5.opt configs/deprecated/example/se.py \
      --cpu-type=O3CPU --caches --l2cache \
      --l1d_size=32kB --l1i_size=32kB \
      --l2_size=2MB --l2_assoc=8 \
      --l2-hit-latency=7 \     # <- from CACTI, in cycles
      --mem-type=DDR4_2400_8x8 --mem-size=4GB \
      --cmd=./bfs --options="-g 18"

  # Alternative — NVSim STT-MRAM L2 (8 MB in same area, 2x slower hits)
  $ ... --l2_size=8MB --l2-hit-latency=14

  # Read results
  $ grep -E "simSeconds|ipc|l2.*miss_rate" m5out/stats.txt



  Task 1. Run both configurations on two GAPBS kernels (e.g. bfs and sssp). Report IPC, L2 miss rate, and
  simSeconds for each.
  Task 2. The MRAM configuration is 4× larger and ~2× slower per hit. For which kernel does that trade win, and
  what property of the kernel determines the outcome?
  Task 3. Re-run the winning configuration with --cpu-type=TimingSimple. The advantage will change in
  magnitude. Explain what out-of-order execution was doing to your Part E Task 1 result.
  Task 4. Write two paragraphs — this is the primary deliverable. (i) Answer the central question from the
  assignment overview, with the evidence from Parts A–E. (ii) State the three assumptions in your simulation
  chain you would attack first if you were the reviewer. [30 % of total marks]
  ⚠ Note: 'STT-MRAM is M× faster' is not a result. 'STT-MRAM is M× faster on bfs, given these device numbers, this cell
  file, this scheduler, and an O3 core' is a result.


Setup & References
Install: ngspice (apt/brew), CACTI 7 and NVSim (make), Ramulator 2.0 (CMake, C++20), gem5 (scons — allow 40 min).
Docker images for all five are on the course page.
Model cards: PTM 45 nm bulk BSIM4 from ptm.asu.edu for Part A. All other parts use the shipped 45 nm configs so
your five results remain comparable.
Tool                Repository / Site                              Primary paper to cite
ngspice             ngspice.sourceforge.io                         PTM BSIM4 — ptm.asu.edu
CACTI 7             github.com/HewlettPackard/cacti                Balasubramonian et al., ACM TACO, vol. 14, no. 2, 2017
NVSim               github.com/SEAL-UCSB/NVSim                     Dong, Xu, Xie & Jouppi, IEEE TCAD, vol. 31, no. 7, 2012
Ramulator 2.0       github.com/CMU-SAFARI/ramulator2               Luo et al., IEEE CAL, vol. 23, no. 1, 2024
DRAMsim3            github.com/umd-memsys/DRAMsim3                 Li et al., IEEE CAL, vol. 19, no. 2, 2020
gem5                gem5.org · learning.gem5.org                   Lowe-Power et al., arXiv:2007.03152, 2020


Accuracy reminders: ngspice ±5 % (model-card limited) · CACTI ±10 % · Ramulator ±10 % · gem5 ±20 %. Errors compound
multiplicatively — report ratios, not absolutes.

# Non-volatile memory simulator
# Pre-release version, r131

target := nvsim

# define tool chain
CXX := g++
RM := rm -f

# define build options
# compile options
CXXFLAGS := -Wall
# link options
LDFLAGS :=
# link librarires
LDLIBS :=

# construct list of .cpp and their corresponding .o and .d files
SRC := $(wildcard *.cpp)
INC :=
DBG :=
OBJ := $(SRC:.cpp=.o)
DEP := Makefile.dep

# file disambiguity is achieved via the .PHONY directive
.PHONY : all clean dbg

all : $(target)

dbg: DBG += -ggdb -g
dbg: $(target)

$(target) : $(OBJ)
	$(CXX) $(LDFLAGS) $^ $(LDLIBS) -o $@

clean :
	$(RM) $(target) $(dep_file) $(OBJ)

.cpp.o :
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(DBG) $(INC) -c $< -o $@

depend $(DEP):
	@echo Makefile - creating dependencies for: $(SRC)
	@$(RM) $(DEP)
	@$(CXX) -E -MM $(INC) $(SRC) >> $(DEP)

ifeq (,$(findstring clean,$(MAKECMDGOALS)))
-include $(DEP)
endif

### Task1: side-by-side 2MB L2

| metric (cache-level) | SRAM `SRAM.cell` 146F2 | STT `assign_STTRAM.cell` 54F2 3k/6k 200uA 40uA read | ratio STT/SRAM |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total area | 6.393 mm² (data 5.944 + tag 0.449) | 3.590 mm² (data 3.142 + tag 0.448) | **0.56x** -44% |
| Hit latency | 0.850 ns (data 753ps + tag+cmp) | 1.591 ns (data 1.449ns) | **1.87x** slower |
| Write latency | 0.520 ns | 10.608 ns | **20.4x** slower |
| Miss latency | 0.251 ns | 1.107 ns | 4.4x |
| Hit dynamic energy | 0.575 nJ | 0.763 nJ | 1.33x |
| Write dynamic energy | 0.531 nJ | 0.435 nJ | 0.82x |
| Leakage | 3196 mW (data 2981 + tag 215) | 425 mW (data 369 + tag 56) | **0.13x** 7.5x lower |
| Data read energy | 561 pJ | 665 pJ | 1.18x |
| Data senseamp | 3.5 ps | 805 ps | dominant |

*SRAM leakage inflated (NVSim HP no power-gating) — ratio still valid.*

### Task2: 2 worse, 2 better — device reason

**Worse:**
- `Write latency` 20x — STT needs 10ns current pulse to switch free layer (`Reset/SetPulse`). SRAM write = drive bitline, flip cross-coupled inverters ~50ps `Charge Latency`.
- `Read latency` 1.9x — current-mode sensing: `Senseamp 805ps` vs SRAM 3ps. Small TMR 2:1 → small ΔI (40uA through 3k vs 6k → ~20mV), needs large/latency sense amp + precharge 429ps vs 52ps.

**Better:**
- `Leakage` 7.5x — MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold/cross-coupled leakage. SRAM `15.9mW/mat` vs STT `23mW/mat` but SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) → total 2981mW vs 369mW.
- `Area` 1.78x denser — 1T-1MTJ 54F2 vs 6T 146F2. Fewer mats, shorter H-tree? Data 2.935x2.025mm vs 2.881x1.090mm.

`Read/write energy` ~ wash — H-tree dominates both (~500pJ/300pJ), cell read 7-14pJ negligible at array level.

### Task3: TMR 2:1 → 3:1 (3k/6k → 4k/12k, keep 40uA read, 200uA write)

Result: almost nothing moves.

```
baseline 3k/6k: hit 1.591ns read 665pJ write 10.608ns 3.590mm²
TMR-high 4k/12k: hit 1.596ns (+5ps +0.3%) read 663pJ (-0.3%) write 10.657ns (+0.5%) area 3.580mm² (-0.3%)
```

Most moved: `read energy` -1.9pJ, noise. Leakage unchanged.

Device reason: TMR headline = `(Roff-Ron)/Ron` → bigger ΔR → bigger sense margin vs `MinSenseVoltage 25mV`, not speed/energy. NVSim read `ReadPower` clamped 145uW, `ReadCurrent` fixed 40uA — higher R → higher V swing but same I, senseamp latency model fixed ~805ps, organization unchanged. At array level TMR buys yield/BER/ecc overhead, not PPA. Need to re-optimize reference current or sense amp to cash TMR for lower read current/power.

### Task4: halve `Reset/SetCurrent` 200uA → 100uA

Result with fixed `CellArea 54F2` + `AccessCMOSWidth 6F`:
```
100uA 6F: hit 1.571ns (-20ps) write 10.588ns (-20ps) leakage 425.0mW (-0.2mW) area 3.590mm² (0%)
100uA 3F: same — area unchanged
```

**Chain (assignment hint):** `I_write ↓ → W_access ↓ (Id ∝ W)` → `cell height ↓` → `cell area ↓` → `array area ↓` → density win you bought NVM for. Also smaller access TX → lower bitline cap/leakage, lower write driver energy.

Why NVSim shows no area change: `assign_STTRAM.cell` fixes `CellArea 54F2` — dominates over transistor footprint at 45nm (`54*45²=0.109µm²` vs `W=6F=270nm*45nm≈0.012µm²`). Model: `area = max(CellArea*F², transistor pitch)`. Halving W still under MTJ pitch, so no win. To see coupling, must scale `CellArea` proportionally or start from transistor-limited cell (e.g., 8F width, aggressive MTJ pitch). In silicon, 200uA needs ~8-10F TX at 45nm, so cell truly TX-limited → halving current → ~30-40% area cut.

Report 100uA case as "NVSim fixed-area artifact; ideal scaled cell would be ~0.07-0.08µm², ~1.4x denser than 200uA" and cite `MemCell::CellScaling`/`SubArray` area calc.

# ponytail: fixed CellArea hides TX scaling, upgrade path = derive CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or use `widthAccessCMOS` scaling model

The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

    62	During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

   132	  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
   133	  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
   134	  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.

\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\

0.60 & 506.73 \\

\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

\begin{table}[H]

\textbf{Capacity} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Leakage (mW)} \\
\midrule
256\,kB & 2.417 & 0.658 & 90.3 \\

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\\[0.5em]
$\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2$

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

\\[1em]

% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Same capacity, same periphery --- different bitcell. What changes?

NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted. Array organisation, peripheral search, and output format are identical; results are only as good as the \texttt{.cell} file. All runs below: \textbf{45\,nm, HP, ReadEDP, Normal access, H-tree, 350\,K, 2\,MB, 64\,B line, 8-way, 512-bit word} --- identical to Part~B. NVSim \texttt{r131} patched for GCC~16 (\texttt{std::data} clash: \texttt{data} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{memData} in \texttt{main.cpp:291,314,327,428}), built binary 424\,KB.

\texttt{SRAM.cell}: 146\,F$^2$, 6T voltage-mode. \texttt{assign\_STTRAM.cell} (assignment spec, adapted to NVSim format): 54\,F$^2$, aspect~2.0, $R_{on}$=3\,k$\Omega$, $R_{off}$=6\,k$\Omega$ (TMR~2:1), current-mode read 40\,$\mu$A/0.25\,V/\,25\,mV sense, 145\,$\mu$W, write Reset/Set 200\,$\mu$A $\times$ 10\,ns, CMOS~6\,F, $V_{drop}$=0.15\,V.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

Device-paper TMR headline buys \textbf{margin/BER}, not speed/energy at array level: larger $\Delta R$ $\rightarrow$ larger sense margin vs 25\,mV offset, improves yield/ECC overhead and allows lower read current or smaller senseamp \textit{if re-optimised} --- but NVSim with fixed ReadPower/ReadCurrent and fixed senseamp keeps latency flat. Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Halve Write Current 200 $\rightarrow$ 100\,$\mu$A}

\begin{lstlisting}
# assign_STTRAM_halfCurrent.cell: Reset/Set 100uA
./nvsim partC_STTRAM_halfCurrent_45nm_2MB.cfg
\end{lstlisting}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{200\,$\mu$A 6F} & \textbf{100\,$\mu$A 6F (3F alt)} & \textbf{Delta} \\
\midrule
Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.590\,mm$^2$ (3.590) & 0\% \\
Hit latency & 1.591\,ns & 1.571\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.588\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.0\,mW & $-$0.05\% \\
Write energy & 0.435\,nJ & 0.433\,nJ & $-$0.5\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task~4: Halved current with fixed CellArea.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.

Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

   286

(2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. % ============================================================
\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}


% ============================================================
\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: SRAM Baseline}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
Access time & 2.902\,ns \\
Cycle time & 2.652\,ns \\
Dynamic read energy & 0.793\,nJ \\
Leakage power (bank) & 562.6\,mW \\
Area (H $\times$ W) & 2.213 $\times$ 5.184\,mm \\
Best Ndwl / Ndbl / Nspd & 4 / 2 / 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1: 2\,MB SRAM L2 baseline at 45\,nm, ED$^2$ optimized.}
\end{table}

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Capacity Sweep (256\,kB -- 16\,MB)}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Capacity} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Leakage (mW)} \\
\midrule
256\,kB & 2.417 & 0.658 & 90.3 \\
512\,kB & 2.485 & 0.679 & 158.1 \\
1\,MB & 2.634 & 0.717 & 293.7 \\
2\,MB & 2.902 & 0.793 & 562.6 \\
4\,MB & 3.531 & 0.930 & 1102.3 \\
8\,MB & 4.473 & 1.220 & 2183.8 \\
16\,MB & 6.362 & 1.742 & 4244.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: CACTI capacity sweep results.}
\end{table}

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule
Pure delay & 2.892 & 0.898 & 4 & 2 \\
Pure area & 3.355 & 0.797 & 2 & 2 \\
ED$^2$ (baseline) & 2.902 & 0.795 & 4 & 2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: Different optimization objectives for 2\,MB SRAM.}
\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

% ============================================================
\section*{Part C --- NVSim: 2\,MB STT-MRAM vs SRAM}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Same capacity, same periphery --- different bitcell. What changes?

NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted. Array organisation, peripheral search, and output format are identical; results are only as good as the \texttt{.cell} file. All runs below: \textbf{45\,nm, HP, ReadEDP, Normal access, H-tree, 350\,K, 2\,MB, 64\,B line, 8-way, 512-bit word} --- identical to Part~B. NVSim \texttt{r131} patched for GCC~16 (\texttt{std::data} clash: \texttt{data} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{memData} in \texttt{main.cpp:291,314,327,428}), built binary 424\,KB.

\texttt{SRAM.cell}: 146\,F$^2$, 6T voltage-mode. \texttt{assign\_STTRAM.cell} (assignment spec, adapted to NVSim format): 54\,F$^2$, aspect~2.0, $R_{on}$=3\,k$\Omega$, $R_{off}$=6\,k$\Omega$ (TMR~2:1), current-mode read 40\,$\mu$A/0.25\,V/\,25\,mV sense, 145\,$\mu$W, write Reset/Set 200\,$\mu$A $\times$ 10\,ns, CMOS~6\,F, $V_{drop}$=0.15\,V.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

Most moved: read energy $-$1.9\,pJ (noise). Device-paper TMR headline buys \textbf{margin/BER}, not speed/energy at array level: larger $\Delta R$ $\rightarrow$ larger sense margin vs 25\,mV offset, improves yield/ECC overhead and allows lower read current or smaller senseamp \textit{if re-optimised} --- but NVSim with fixed ReadPower/ReadCurrent and fixed senseamp keeps latency flat. Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.

\subsection*{Task 4: Halve Write Current 200 $\rightarrow$ 100\,$\mu$A}

\begin{lstlisting}

./nvsim partC_STTRAM_halfCurrent_45nm_2MB.cfg
\end{lstlisting}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{200\,$\mu$A 6F} & \textbf{100\,$\mu$A 6F (3F alt)} & \textbf{Delta} \\
\midrule
Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.590\,mm$^2$ (3.590) & 0\% \\
Hit latency & 1.591\,ns & 1.571\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.588\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.0\,mW & $-$0.05\% \\
Write energy & 0.435\,nJ & 0.433\,nJ & $-$0.5\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task~4: Halved current with fixed CellArea.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.

Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

   281	%% ------------------------------------------------------------
   282	\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}
   283	
   284	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   285	
   286	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).
   287	
   288	%% ------------------------------------------------------------
   289	\subsection*{Task 3: TMR 2:1 $\rightarrow$ 3:1 ($R_{on}$=4\,k, $R_{off}$=12\,k)}
   290	
   291	Keep 40\,$\mu$A read, 200\,$\mu$A write, 54\,F$^2$:
   292	\begin{lstlisting}
   293	# assign_STTRAM_TMRhigh.cell: 4000/12000 ohm
   294	./nvsim partC_STTRAM_TMRhigh_45nm_2MB.cfg
   295	\end{lstlisting}
   296	
   297	\begin{table}[H]
   298	\centering
   299	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
   300	\toprule
   301	\textbf{} & \textbf{3k/6k (2:1)} & \textbf{4k/12k (3:1)} & \textbf{Delta} \\
   302	\midrule
   303	Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.580\,mm$^2$ & $-$0.3\% \\
   304	Hit latency & 1.591\,ns (1449\,ps data) & 1.596\,ns (1454\,ps) & +5\,ps \\
   305	Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.657\,ns & +0.5\% \\
   306	Hit energy & 0.763\,nJ (665\,pJ data) & 0.761\,nJ (663\,pJ) & $-$0.3\% \\
   307	Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.2\,mW & 0 \\
   308	\bottomrule
   309	\end{tabular}
   310	\caption{Task~3: Higher TMR at same absolute write current. No PPA win.}
   311	\end{table}
   312	
   313	Most moved: read energy $-$1.9\,pJ (noise). Device-paper TMR headline buys \textbf{margin/BER}, not speed/energy at array level: larger $\Delta R$ $\rightarrow$ larger sense margin vs 25\,mV offset, improves yield/ECC overhead and allows lower read current or smaller senseamp \textit{if re-optimised} --- but NVSim with fixed ReadPower/ReadCurrent and fixed senseamp keeps latency flat. Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.
   314	
   315	%% ------------------------------------------------------------
   316	\subsection*{Task 4: Halve Write Current 200 $\rightarrow$ 100\,$\mu$A}
   317	
   318	\begin{lstlisting}
   319	# assign_STTRAM_halfCurrent.cell: Reset/Set 100uA
   320	./nvsim partC_STTRAM_halfCurrent_45nm_2MB.cfg
   321	\end{lstlisting}
   322	
   323	\begin{table}[H]
   324	\centering
   325	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
   326	\toprule
   327	\textbf{} & \textbf{200\,$\mu$A 6F} & \textbf{100\,$\mu$A 6F (3F alt)} & \textbf{Delta} \\
   328	\midrule
   329	Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.590\,mm$^2$ (3.590) & 0\% \\
   330	Hit latency & 1.591\,ns & 1.571\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
   331	Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.588\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
   332	Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.0\,mW & $-$0.05\% \\
   333	Write energy & 0.435\,nJ & 0.433\,nJ & $-$0.5\% \\
   334	\bottomrule
   335	\end{tabular}
   336	\caption{Task~4: Halved current with fixed CellArea.}
   337	\end{table}
   338	
   339	\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.
   340	
   341	Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.
   342

\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}


% ============================================================
\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: SRAM Baseline}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
Access time & 2.902\,ns \\
Cycle time & 2.652\,ns \\
Dynamic read energy & 0.793\,nJ \\
Leakage power (bank) & 562.6\,mW \\
Area (H $\times$ W) & 2.213 $\times$ 5.184\,mm \\
Best Ndwl / Ndbl / Nspd & 4 / 2 / 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1: 2\,MB SRAM L2 baseline at 45\,nm, ED$^2$ optimized.}
\end{table}

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Capacity Sweep (256\,kB -- 16\,MB)}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Capacity} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Leakage (mW)} \\
\midrule
256\,kB & 2.417 & 0.658 & 90.3 \\
512\,kB & 2.485 & 0.679 & 158.1 \\
1\,MB & 2.634 & 0.717 & 293.7 \\
2\,MB & 2.902 & 0.793 & 562.6 \\
4\,MB & 3.531 & 0.930 & 1102.3 \\
8\,MB & 4.473 & 1.220 & 2183.8 \\
16\,MB & 6.362 & 1.742 & 4244.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: CACTI capacity sweep results.}
\end{table}

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule
Pure delay & 2.892 & 0.898 & 4 & 2 \\
Pure area & 3.355 & 0.797 & 2 & 2 \\
ED$^2$ (baseline) & 2.902 & 0.795 & 4 & 2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: Different optimization objectives for 2\,MB SRAM.}
\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

   273	Read latency & 753\,ps & 1449\,ps \\
   274	\; H-tree / Mat & 467 / 287\,ps & 231 / 1218\,ps \\
   275	\; sense / precharge & 3.5 / 52\,ps & 805 / 429\,ps \\
   276	Write latency & 520\,ps & 10.608\,ns \\
   277	& & (10\,ns pulse) \\
   278	Read energy & 561\,pJ & 665\,pJ \\
   279	\; H-tree / Mat & 502 / 7.4\,pJ/mat & 298 / 91.7\,pJ/mat \\
   280	Write energy & 518\,pJ & 390\,pJ \\
   281	Leakage & 2981\,mW total & 369\,mW total \\
   282	& 11.65\,mW/mat & 23.09\,mW/mat \\
   283	\midrule
   284	Tag array & 0.449\,mm$^2$, 251\,ps, 14\,pJ & 0.448\,mm$^2$, 1107\,ps, 98\,pJ \\
   285	& 215\,mW & 56\,mW \\
   286	\bottomrule
   287	\end{tabular}
   288	\caption{Data/tag breakdown. *Fewer banks optimal for MRAM; tag similar, data dominates.}
   289	\end{table}
   290	
   291	\noindent SRAM leakage is HP, no power-gating (CACTI would be lower); ratio still valid.
   292	
   293	%% ------------------------------------------------------------
   294	\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}
   295	
   296	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   297	
   298	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).
   299	
   300	%% ------------------------------------------------------------
   301	\subsection*{Task 3: TMR 2:1 $\rightarrow$ 3:1 ($R_{on}$=4\,k, $R_{off}$=12\,k)}
   302	
   303	Keep 40\,$\mu$A read, 200\,$\mu$A write, 54\,F$^2$:
   304	\begin{lstlisting}
   305	# assign_STTRAM_TMRhigh.cell: 4000/12000 ohm
   306	./nvsim partC_STTRAM_TMRhigh_45nm_2MB.cfg
   307	\end{lstlisting}
   308	
   309	\begin{table}[H]
   310	\centering
   311	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
   312	\toprule
   313	\textbf{} & \textbf{3k/6k (2:1)} & \textbf{4k/12k (3:1)} & \textbf{Delta} \\
   314	\midrule
   315	Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.580\,mm$^2$ & $-$0.3\% \\
   316	Hit latency & 1.591\,ns (1449\,ps data) & 1.596\,ns (1454\,ps) & +5\,ps \\
   317	Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.657\,ns & +0.5\% \\
   318	Hit energy & 0.763\,nJ (665\,pJ data) & 0.761\,nJ (663\,pJ) & $-$0.3\% \\
   319	Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.2\,mW & 0 \\
   320	\bottomrule
   321	\end{tabular}
   322	\caption{Task~3: Higher TMR at same absolute write current. No PPA win.}
   323	\end{table}
   324	
   325	Most moved: read energy $-$1.9\,pJ (noise). Device-paper TMR headline buys \textbf{margin/BER}, not speed/energy at array level: larger $\Delta R$ $\rightarrow$ larger sense margin vs 25\,mV offset, improves yield/ECC overhead and allows lower read current or smaller senseamp \textit{if re-optimised} --- but NVSim with fixed ReadPower/ReadCurrent and fixed senseamp keeps latency flat. Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.

---Makefile---
# Non-volatile memory simulator
# Pre-release version, r131

target := nvsim

# define tool chain
CXX := g++
RM := rm -f

# define build options
# compile options
CXXFLAGS := -Wall
# link options
LDFLAGS :=
# link librarires
LDLIBS :=

# construct list of .cpp and their corresponding .o and .d files
SRC := $(wildcard *.cpp)
INC :=
DBG :=
OBJ := $(SRC:.cpp=.o)
DEP := Makefile.dep

# file disambiguity is achieved via the .PHONY directive
.PHONY : all clean dbg

all : $(target)

dbg: DBG += -ggdb -g
dbg: $(target)

$(target) : $(OBJ)
	$(CXX) $(LDFLAGS) $^ $(LDLIBS) -o $@

clean :
	$(RM) $(target) $(dep_file) $(OBJ)

.cpp.o :
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(DBG) $(INC) -c $< -o $@

depend $(DEP):
	@echo Makefile - creating dependencies for: $(SRC)
	@$(RM) $(DEP)
	@$(CXX) -E -MM $(INC) $(SRC) >> $(DEP)

ifeq (,$(findstring clean,$(MAKECMDGOALS)))
-include $(DEP)
endif
---EOF---

\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule

\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

\end{document}

(2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. % ============================================================
\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}


% ============================================================
\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: SRAM Baseline}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

% ============================================================
\section*{Part C --- NVSim: 2\,MB STT-MRAM vs SRAM}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Same capacity, same periphery --- different bitcell. What changes?

NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted. Array organisation, peripheral search, and output format are identical; results are only as good as the \texttt{.cell} file. All runs below: \textbf{45\,nm, HP, ReadEDP, Normal access, H-tree, 350\,K, 2\,MB, 64\,B line, 8-way, 512-bit word} --- identical to Part~B. NVSim \texttt{r131} patched for GCC~16 (\texttt{std::data} clash: \texttt{data} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{memData} in \texttt{main.cpp:291,314,327,428}), built binary 424\,KB.

\texttt{SRAM.cell}: 146\,F$^2$, 6T voltage-mode. \texttt{assign\_STTRAM.cell} (assignment spec, adapted to NVSim format): 54\,F$^2$, aspect~2.0, $R_{on}$=3\,k$\Omega$, $R_{off}$=6\,k$\Omega$ (TMR~2:1), current-mode read 40\,$\mu$A/0.25\,V/\,25\,mV sense, 145\,$\mu$W, write Reset/Set 200\,$\mu$A $\times$ 10\,ns, CMOS~6\,F, $V_{drop}$=0.15\,V.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

\subsection*{Task 3: TMR 2:1 $\rightarrow$ 3:1 ($R_{on}$=4\,k, $R_{off}$=12\,k)}

Keep 40\,$\mu$A read, 200\,$\mu$A write, 54\,F$^2$:
\begin{lstlisting}
# assign_STTRAM_TMRhigh.cell: 4000/12000 ohm
./nvsim partC_STTRAM_TMRhigh_45nm_2MB.cfg
\end{lstlisting}

\begin{table}[H]

\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}

 & \textbf{3k/6k (TMR 2:1)} & \textbf{4k/12k (TMR 3:1)} & \textbf{Delta} \\
\midrule
Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.580\,mm$^2$ & $-$0.3\% \\
Hit latency & 1.591\,ns & 1.596\,ns & +5\,ps \\
Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.657\,ns & +0.5\% \\
Hit energy & 0.763\,nJ & 0.761\,nJ & $-$0.3\% \\
Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.2\,mW & 0\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task~3: Higher TMR at same write current. No PPA win.}
\end{table}

Most moved: read energy $-$1.9\,pJ (noise). Device-paper TMR headline buys \textbf{margin/BER}, not speed/energy at array level: larger $\Delta R$ $\rightarrow$ larger sense margin vs 25\,mV offset, improves yield/ECC overhead and allows lower read current or smaller senseamp \textit{if re-optimised} --- but NVSim with fixed ReadPower/ReadCurrent and fixed senseamp keeps latency flat. Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.
