\subsection*{Task 4: Halve Write Current 200 $\rightarrow$ 100\,$\mu$A}

\begin{lstlisting}
# assign_STTRAM_halfCurrent.cell: Reset/Set 100uA
./nvsim partC_STTRAM_halfCurrent_45nm_2MB.cfg
\end{lstlisting}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
 & \textbf{200\,$\mu$A, 6\,F} & \textbf{100\,$\mu$A, 6\,F} & \textbf{Delta} \\
\midrule
Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 0\% \\
Hit latency & 1.591\,ns & 1.571\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.588\,ns & $-$20\,ps \\
Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.0\,mW & $-$0.2\,mW \\
Write energy & 0.435\,nJ & 0.433\,nJ & $-$0.5\% \\
Read energy & 0.763\,nJ & 0.762\,nJ & $-$0.1\% \\  
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task~4: Halved write current (fixed 54\,F$^2$ cell) --- zero area change is artefact.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.

Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

\end{document}

Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   292	
   293	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

   351	\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.
   352	
   353	Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

   290	
   291	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   292	
   293	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.

   353	Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

   289	\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}
   290	
   291	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   292	
   293	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

% ============================================================
\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

\midrule

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule

Pure area & 3.355 & 0.797 & 2 & 2 \\
ED$^2$ (baseline) & 2.902 & 0.795 & 4 & 2 \\
\bottomrule

\caption{Task 3: Different optimization objectives for 2\,MB SRAM.}
\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

\textbf{Central question:} Same capacity, same periphery --- different bitcell. What changes?

NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted. Array organisation, peripheral search, and output format are identical; results are only as good as the \texttt{.cell} file. All runs below: \textbf{45\,nm, HP, ReadEDP, Normal access, H-tree, 350\,K, 2\,MB, 64\,B line, 8-way, 512-bit word} --- identical to Part~B. NVSim \texttt{r131} patched for GCC~16 (\texttt{std::data} clash: \texttt{data} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{memData} in \texttt{main.cpp:291,314,327,428}), built binary 424\,KB.

\texttt{SRAM.cell}: 146\,F$^2$, 6T voltage-mode. \texttt{assign\_STTRAM.cell} (assignment spec, adapted to NVSim format): 54\,F$^2$, aspect~2.0, $R_{on}$=3\,k$\Omega$, $R_{off}$=6\,k$\Omega$ (TMR~2:1), current-mode read 40\,$\mu$A/0.25\,V/\,25\,mV sense, 145\,$\mu$W, write Reset/Set 200\,$\mu$A $\times$ 10\,ns, CMOS~6\,F, $V_{drop}$=0.15\,V.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.

Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch).    289	%% ------------------------------------------------------------
   290	\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}
   291	
   292	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   293	
   294	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).
   295

   324	Most moved: read energy $-$1.9\,pJ (noise). Device-paper TMR headline buys \textbf{margin/BER}, not speed/energy at array level: larger $\Delta R$ $\rightarrow$ larger sense margin vs 25\,mV offset, improves yield/ECC overhead and allows lower read current or smaller senseamp \textit{if re-optimised} --- but NVSim with fixed ReadPower/ReadCurrent and fixed senseamp keeps latency flat. Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.

   353	
   354	\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.
   355	
   356	Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

# Non-volatile memory simulator
# Pre-release version, r131

target := nvsim

# define tool chain
CXX := g++
RM := rm -f

# define build options
# compile options
CXXFLAGS := -Wall -std=c++11
# link options
LDFLAGS :=
# link librarires
LDLIBS :=

# construct list of .cpp and their corresponding .o and .d files
SRC := $(wildcard *.cpp)
INC :=
DBG :=
OBJ := $(SRC:.cpp=.o)
DEP := Makefile.dep

# file disambiguity is achieved via the .PHONY directive
.PHONY : all clean dbg

all : $(target)

dbg: DBG += -ggdb -g
dbg: $(target)

$(target) : $(OBJ)
	$(CXX) $(LDFLAGS) $^ $(LDLIBS) -o $@

clean :
	$(RM) $(target) $(dep_file) $(OBJ)

.cpp.o :
	$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $(DBG) $(INC) -c $< -o $@

depend $(DEP):
	@echo Makefile - creating dependencies for: $(SRC)
	@$(RM) $(DEP)
	@$(CXX) -E -MM $(INC) $(SRC) >> $(DEP)

ifeq (,$(findstring clean,$(MAKECMDGOALS)))
-include $(DEP)
endif

   292	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   293	
   294	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.
   355	
   356	Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.

   353	
   354	\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.
   355	
   356	Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54\,F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($54F^2=0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$); model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch). Even scaling Width 6F$\rightarrow$3F keeps MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current $\rightarrow$ $\sim$30--40\% area cut if CellArea were derived. \textbf{Report as fixed-area artefact}; ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser than 200\,$\mu$A. Enable by deriving CellArea from AccessCMOSWidth or enabling \texttt{MemCell::CellScaling}.
   357	
   358	\end{document}

   291	
   292	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   293

(2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. % ============================================================
\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}


% ============================================================
\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: SRAM Baseline}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
Access time & 2.902\,ns \\
Cycle time & 2.652\,ns \\
Dynamic read energy & 0.793\,nJ \\
Leakage power (bank) & 562.6\,mW \\
Area (H $\times$ W) & 2.213 $\times$ 5.184\,mm \\
Best Ndwl / Ndbl / Nspd & 4 / 2 / 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1: 2\,MB SRAM L2 baseline at 45\,nm, ED$^2$ optimized.}
\end{table}

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Capacity Sweep (256\,kB -- 16\,MB)}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Capacity} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Leakage (mW)} \\
\midrule
256\,kB & 2.417 & 0.658 & 90.3 \\
512\,kB & 2.485 & 0.679 & 158.1 \\
1\,MB & 2.634 & 0.717 & 293.7 \\
2\,MB & 2.902 & 0.793 & 562.6 \\
4\,MB & 3.531 & 0.930 & 1102.3 \\
8\,MB & 4.473 & 1.220 & 2183.8 \\
16\,MB & 6.362 & 1.742 & 4244.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: CACTI capacity sweep results.}
\end{table}

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule
Pure delay & 2.892 & 0.898 & 4 & 2 \\
Pure area & 3.355 & 0.797 & 2 & 2 \\
ED$^2$ (baseline) & 2.902 & 0.795 & 4 & 2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: Different optimization objectives for 2\,MB SRAM.}
\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

% ============================================================
\section*{Part C --- NVSim: 2\,MB STT-MRAM vs SRAM}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Same capacity, same periphery --- different bitcell. What changes?

NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted. Array organisation, peripheral search, and output format are identical; results are only as good as the \texttt{.cell} file. All runs below: \textbf{45\,nm, HP, ReadEDP, Normal access, H-tree, 350\,K, 2\,MB, 64\,B line, 8-way, 512-bit word} --- identical to Part~B. NVSim \texttt{r131} patched for GCC~16 (\texttt{std::data} clash: \texttt{data} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{memData} in \texttt{main.cpp:291,314,327,428}), built binary 424\,KB.

\texttt{SRAM.cell}: 146\,F$^2$, 6T voltage-mode. \texttt{assign\_STTRAM.cell} (assignment spec, adapted to NVSim format): 54\,F$^2$, aspect~2.0, $R_{on}$=3\,k$\Omega$, $R_{off}$=6\,k$\Omega$ (TMR~2:1), current-mode read 40\,$\mu$A/0.25\,V/\,25\,mV sense, 145\,$\mu$W, write Reset/Set 200\,$\mu$A $\times$ 10\,ns, CMOS~6\,F, $V_{drop}$=0.15\,V.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

   291	\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}
   292	
   293	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   294	
   295	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

% ============================================================
\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}


% ============================================================
\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: SRAM Baseline}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
Access time & 2.902\,ns \\
Cycle time & 2.652\,ns \\
Dynamic read energy & 0.793\,nJ \\
Leakage power (bank) & 562.6\,mW \\
Area (H $\times$ W) & 2.213 $\times$ 5.184\,mm \\
Best Ndwl / Ndbl / Nspd & 4 / 2 / 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1: 2\,MB SRAM L2 baseline at 45\,nm, ED$^2$ optimized.}
\end{table}

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Capacity Sweep (256\,kB -- 16\,MB)}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Capacity} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Leakage (mW)} \\
\midrule
256\,kB & 2.417 & 0.658 & 90.3 \\
512\,kB & 2.485 & 0.679 & 158.1 \\
1\,MB & 2.634 & 0.717 & 293.7 \\
2\,MB & 2.902 & 0.793 & 562.6 \\
4\,MB & 3.531 & 0.930 & 1102.3 \\
8\,MB & 4.473 & 1.220 & 2183.8 \\
16\,MB & 6.362 & 1.742 & 4244.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: CACTI capacity sweep results.}
\end{table}

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule
Pure delay & 2.892 & 0.898 & 4 & 2 \\
Pure area & 3.355 & 0.797 & 2 & 2 \\
ED$^2$ (baseline) & 2.902 & 0.795 & 4 & 2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: Different optimization objectives for 2\,MB SRAM.}
\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

% ============================================================
\section*{Part C --- NVSim: 2\,MB STT-MRAM vs SRAM}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Same capacity, same periphery --- different bitcell. What changes?

NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted. Array organisation, peripheral search, and output format are identical; results are only as good as the \texttt{.cell} file. All runs below: \textbf{45\,nm, HP, ReadEDP, Normal access, H-tree, 350\,K, 2\,MB, 64\,B line, 8-way, 512-bit word} --- identical to Part~B. NVSim \texttt{r131} patched for GCC~16 (\texttt{std::data} clash: \texttt{data} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{memData} in \texttt{main.cpp:291,314,327,428}), built binary 424\,KB.

\texttt{SRAM.cell}: 146\,F$^2$, 6T voltage-mode. \texttt{assign\_STTRAM.cell} (assignment spec, adapted to NVSim format): 54\,F$^2$, aspect~2.0, $R_{on}$=3\,k$\Omega$, $R_{off}$=6\,k$\Omega$ (TMR~2:1), current-mode read 40\,$\mu$A/0.25\,V/\,25\,mV sense, 145\,$\mu$W, write Reset/Set 200\,$\mu$A $\times$ 10\,ns, CMOS~6\,F, $V_{drop}$=0.15\,V.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

Keep 40\,$\mu$A read, 200\,$\mu$A write, 54\,F$^2$:

Most moved: read energy $-$1.9\,pJ (noise). Device-paper TMR headline buys \textbf{margin/BER}, not speed/energy at array level: larger $\Delta R$ $\rightarrow$ larger sense margin vs 25\,mV offset, improves yield/ECC overhead and allows lower read current or smaller senseamp \textit{if re-optimised} --- but NVSim with fixed ReadPower/ReadCurrent and fixed senseamp keeps latency flat. Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.

\subsection*{Task 4: Halve Write Current 200 $\rightarrow$ 100\,$\mu$A}

\begin{lstlisting}
# assign_STTRAM_halfCurrent.cell: Reset/Set 100uA
./nvsim partC_STTRAM_halfCurrent_45nm_2MB.cfg
\end{lstlisting}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{200\,$\mu$A (6\,F)} & \textbf{100\,$\mu$A (6\,F)} & \textbf{Delta} \\
\midrule
Total area & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 3.590\,mm$^2$ & 0\% \\
Read (hit) latency & 1.591\,ns & 1.571\,ns & $-$1.26\% ($-$20\,ps) \\
Write latency & 10.608\,ns & 10.588\,ns & $-$0.19\% ($-$20\,ps) \\
Read energy & 0.763\,nJ & 0.762\,nJ & $-$0.13\% \\
Write energy & 0.435\,nJ & 0.433\,nJ & \textbf{$-$0.46\%} \\
Leakage & 425.2\,mW & 425.0\,mW & $-$0.05\% \\
Access width & 6\,F & 6\,F (3\,F alt: same) & --- (no change) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task~4: Halved write current. Most moved: write energy $-$0.46\%; area 0\% is artefact (fixed 54\,F$^2$).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.

Why NVSim shows \textbf{zero area change}: \texttt{CellArea=54F$^2$} is fixed and dominates \texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm (\texttt{54F$^2$}=0.109\,$\mu$m$^2$ vs $W$=6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$). Model uses $\max$(CellArea, transistor pitch), so even 6F$\to$3F stays MTJ pitch-limited. In silicon 200\,\mu A needs $\sim$8--10F at 45\,nm, so cell is TX-limited; halving current would cut $\sim$30--40\% area if CellArea were derived. Report as fixed-area artefact (ideal scaled cell $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$, $\sim$1.4$\times$ denser).

\end{document}

\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}

\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

\midrule

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule

ED$^2$ (baseline) & 2.902 & 0.795 & 4 & 2 \\

\caption{Task 3: Different optimization objectives for 2\,MB SRAM.}
\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

   288	%% ------------------------------------------------------------
   289	\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}
   290	
   291	\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.
   292	
   293	\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

% ============================================================
\section*{Part A --- ngspice: 6T SRAM Read Margin}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Does the bitcell actually read correctly, at 0.7\,V and 85\,$^\circ$C?

A 6T SRAM cell was simulated using a 45\,nm HP PTM BSIM4 model (\texttt{45nm\_HP.pm}) in ngspice. The wordline (WL) ramps from 0\,V to $V_{DD}$=1.1\,V at $t=1$\,ns via a PWL source. The bitlines are precharged to $V_{DD}$ and the cell stores $Q=0$, $Q_B=V_{DD}$.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: $\Delta V$(BL,BLB) at $t=2$\,ns}

\textbf{Method:} Transient analysis (\texttt{tran 5p 4n uic}) with initial conditions $v(Q)=0$, $v(Q_B)=V_{DD}$. The differential voltage $\Delta V = v(BLB) - v(BL)$ was computed as a separate vector and measured at $t=2$\,ns.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ at $t=2$\,ns & \textbf{729.86\,mV} \\
$q_{\max}$ (read disturb) & 205.52\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1 measurement results at 27\,$^\circ$C, $V_{DD}=1.1$\,V.}
\end{table}

\textbf{Comparison with reference:} The measured $\Delta V$ = 729.86\,mV is $\sim$10.6$\times$ larger than the 69\,mV reference value from Lecture~1. The large differential indicates the cell reads correctly with ample margin. The 69\,mV reference likely corresponds to a worst-case or minimum-margin scenario with different sizing or operating conditions.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Plot $v(Q)$ and Effect of Doubling MA1/MA2}

\textbf{Base case (W=0.16\,$\mu$m):}
During the read, the Q node is disturbed from 0\,V up to $q_{\max}=205.52$\,mV at $t=1.0575$\,ns. This is the classic \textbf{read disturb} --- current flows from the precharged BL through MA1 and MN1, pulling Q above ground. The cross-coupled inverter holds the data because MN1 (W=0.20\,$\mu$m) is stronger than MA1 (W=0.16\,$\mu$m), keeping the voltage divider favorable.

\textbf{After doubling MA1/MA2 to W=0.24\,$\mu$m:}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{W=0.16\,$\mu$m} & \textbf{W=0.24\,$\mu$m} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 852.34 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 271.22 \\
Cell ratio ($W_{MA}/W_{MN}$) & 0.80 & 1.20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: Effect of doubling access transistor width.}
\end{table}

With W$_{MA}$=0.24\,$\mu$m and W$_{MN}$=0.20\,$\mu$m, the cell ratio drops to 1.2 --- dangerously close to 1. The read disturb increases by 32\% (271\,mV vs 206\,mV), pushing Q closer to the inverter trip point. At higher temperatures or lower $V_{DD}$, this configuration would likely \textbf{fail} (read upset), as the assignment predicts.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ Sweep}

$V_{DD}$ was swept from 1.1\,V down to 0.6\,V in 50\,mV steps using a \texttt{.control} loop in ngspice.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{cc}
\toprule
\textbf{$V_{DD}$ (V)} & \textbf{$\Delta V$ at 2\,ns (mV)} \\
\midrule
1.10 & 729.86 \\
1.05 & 715.27 \\
1.00 & 698.66 \\
0.95 & 679.88 \\
0.90 & 658.87 \\
0.85 & 635.58 \\
0.80 & 610.10 \\
0.75 & 582.63 \\
0.70 & 554.08 \\
0.65 & 527.18 \\
0.60 & 506.73 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: $\Delta V$ vs $V_{DD}$ sweep results.}
\end{table}

$\Delta V$ decreases monotonically with $V_{DD}$ but remains well above 25\,mV across the entire range (minimum $\Delta V$ = 506.73\,mV at $V_{DD}$=0.6\,V). With the given model and sizing, the bitcell maintains sufficient read margin even at 0.6\,V. The 25\,mV sense-amp offset threshold is never crossed in this sweep, indicating robust cell design for this voltage range.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Repeat at $T=85\,^\circ$C}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{27\,$^\circ$C} & \textbf{85\,$^\circ$C} \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ (mV) & 729.86 & 582.12 \\
$q_{\max}$ (mV) & 205.52 & 220.76 \\
\midrule
$\Delta V$ change & --- & $-$20.2\% \\
$q_{\max}$ change & --- & $+$7.4\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 4: Temperature comparison (27\,$^\circ$C vs 85\,$^\circ$C).}
\end{table}

\textbf{Analysis:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$\Delta V$ decreased by $\sim$148\,mV (20\%):} Carrier mobility degrades with temperature ($\mu \propto T^{-1.5}$), reducing the drive current of the access transistors and slowing the bitline discharge.
  \item \textbf{$q_{\max}$ increased by $\sim$15\,mV (7\%):} The read disturb worsens because the pull-down NMOS (MN1) weakens more than the access transistor, shifting the voltage divider in favor of Q rising.
  \item \textbf{Which sets the failure?} The \textbf{sense-amp offset} moved more relative to its margin. While $\Delta V$ dropped 20\%, it remains 582\,mV --- far above 25\,mV. The real concern at elevated temperature is the \textbf{read disturb} ($q_{\max}$ rising). If the cell were sized closer to failure, temperature-induced mobility degradation would push $q_{\max}$ past the inverter trip point before the sense-amp offset becomes the bottleneck.
\end{itemize}


% ============================================================
\section*{Part B --- CACTI: 2 MB SRAM L2 Sizing}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} How fast, how big, and how leaky is a 2 MB SRAM L2 at 45\,nm?

CACTI 7 was used to model a 2\,MB SRAM L2 cache at the 45\,nm technology node. The configuration: 64\,B block size, 8-way set-associative, 4 banks, ITRS-HP cell/peripheral types, ED$^2$ optimization, cycle-time-weighted objective.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 1: SRAM Baseline}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Value} \\
\midrule
Access time & 2.902\,ns \\
Cycle time & 2.652\,ns \\
Dynamic read energy & 0.793\,nJ \\
Leakage power (bank) & 562.6\,mW \\
Area (H $\times$ W) & 2.213 $\times$ 5.184\,mm \\
Best Ndwl / Ndbl / Nspd & 4 / 2 / 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 1: 2\,MB SRAM L2 baseline at 45\,nm, ED$^2$ optimized.}
\end{table}

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Capacity Sweep (256\,kB -- 16\,MB)}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Capacity} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Leakage (mW)} \\
\midrule
256\,kB & 2.417 & 0.658 & 90.3 \\
512\,kB & 2.485 & 0.679 & 158.1 \\
1\,MB & 2.634 & 0.717 & 293.7 \\
2\,MB & 2.902 & 0.793 & 562.6 \\
4\,MB & 3.531 & 0.930 & 1102.3 \\
8\,MB & 4.473 & 1.220 & 2183.8 \\
16\,MB & 6.362 & 1.742 & 4244.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 2: CACTI capacity sweep results.}
\end{table}

Access time increases approximately linearly with $\log_2$(capacity). Each doubling adds $\sim$0.2--0.5\,ns, consistent with Amrutur \& Horowitz's ``one gate delay per doubling'' observation, though the exact scaling depends on the H-tree depth and bank organization.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 3: Optimization Objective Comparison}

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Objective} & \textbf{Access (ns)} & \textbf{Energy (nJ)} & \textbf{Ndwl} & \textbf{Ndbl} \\
\midrule
Pure delay & 2.892 & 0.898 & 4 & 2 \\
Pure area & 3.355 & 0.797 & 2 & 2 \\
ED$^2$ (baseline) & 2.902 & 0.795 & 4 & 2 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Task 3: Different optimization objectives for 2\,MB SRAM.}
\end{table}

The optimal organisation changes because each objective trades different physical resources: delay minimisation favours wider H-trees (higher Ndwl) and more parallel subarrays; area minimisation favours fewer splits (lower Ndwl) with denser mats; ED$^2$ balances both.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 4: Bitline Delay Hand-Check}

From Task 1, CACTI reports a bitline delay of \textbf{0.407\,ns}.

Using the hand-calculated estimate from Lecture~4:
\begin{equation*}
\Delta t_{BL} \approx 0.38 \cdot R \cdot C \cdot L^2
\end{equation*}

The discrepancy arises because CACTI additionally models: (1)~non-linear capacitance coupling between adjacent bitlines, (2)~sense-amplifier offset and regenerative delay, (3)~wire resistance and inductance in the H-tree routing, and (4)~process-variation-aware timing margins. These effects are absent from the simplified $0.38 \cdot RC \cdot L^2$ formula.

% ============================================================
\section*{Part C --- NVSim: 2\,MB STT-MRAM vs SRAM}
% ============================================================

\textbf{Central question:} Same capacity, same periphery --- different bitcell. What changes?

NVSim is CACTI with the bitcell model extracted. Array organisation, peripheral search, and output format are identical; results are only as good as the \texttt{.cell} file. All runs below: \textbf{45\,nm, HP, ReadEDP, Normal access, H-tree, 350\,K, 2\,MB, 64\,B line, 8-way, 512-bit word} --- identical to Part~B. NVSim \texttt{r131} patched for GCC~16 (\texttt{std::data} clash: \texttt{data} $\rightarrow$ \texttt{memData} in \texttt{main.cpp:291,314,327,428}), built binary 424\,KB.

\texttt{SRAM.cell}: 146\,F$^2$, 6T voltage-mode. \texttt{assign\_STTRAM.cell} (assignment spec, adapted to NVSim format): 54\,F$^2$, aspect~2.0, $R_{on}$=3\,k$\Omega$, $R_{off}$=6\,k$\Omega$ (TMR~2:1), current-mode read 40\,$\mu$A/0.25\,V/\,25\,mV sense, 145\,$\mu$W, write Reset/Set 200\,$\mu$A $\times$ 10\,ns, CMOS~6\,F, $V_{drop}$=0.15\,V.

%% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection*{Task 2: Two Dramatically Worse, Two Dramatically Better}

\textbf{Worse:} (1)~\textbf{Write latency 20.4$\times$} --- STT needs 10\,ns spin-transfer pulse to switch the free layer (Reset/SetPulse); SRAM flips cross-coupled inverters in $\sim$65\,ps charge. Device term: critical switching current $I_{c0}$ and pulse width set by STT dynamics, not RC. (2)~\textbf{Read latency 1.87$\times$} (miss 4.4$\times$) --- current-mode sensing: $\Delta I \approx$ 40\,$\mu$A$\cdot$(1/3k$-$1/6k)$\cdot$R$\rightarrow$ $\sim$20\,mV vs $>$200\,mV SRAM swing. TMR~2:1 $\rightarrow$ small $\Delta V$, senseamp 805\,ps vs 3.5\,ps + precharge 429\,ps vs 52\,ps.

\textbf{Better:} (1)~\textbf{Leakage 7.5$\times$ lower} --- MTJ non-volatile, no 6T subthreshold nor cross-coupled contention; SRAM needs 256 mats (large area) $\rightarrow$ 2981\,mW vs 369\,mW despite higher per-mat leakage. (2)~\textbf{Area 1.78$\times$ denser} --- 1T-1MTJ 54\,F$^2$ vs 6T 146\,F$^2$ (2.7$\times$ cell); array $\sim$44\% smaller, shorter H-tree in one dimension. Read/write energy $\sim$wash (H-tree dominates 300--500\,pJ; cell read 7--15\,pJ negligible at array level).

Absolute $R$ higher even slightly hurts (more $IR$ drop). Array must co-optimise reference current/senseamp to monetise TMR.

\end{table}

\textbf{Mechanism --- the single most important NVM coupling:} $I_{write} \downarrow \rightarrow W_{access} \downarrow$ ($I_d \propto W$) $\rightarrow$ cell height/pitch $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ CellArea ($F^2$) $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ array area $\downarrow$ $\rightarrow$ the density advantage you bought the technology for. Smaller TX also cuts bitline cap, leakage, and driver energy.

Why \textbf{zero area}: \texttt{CellArea=54F$^2$} fixed dominates
\texttt{AccessCMOSWidth} at 45\,nm ($0.109\,\mu$m$^2$ vs 6F $\approx$0.012\,$\mu$m$^2$).
Model $\max$(CellArea, TX pitch) $\rightarrow$ 6F$\to$3F still MTJ-limited.
Si: 200\,$\mu$A needs $\sim$8--10F $\rightarrow$ TX-limited; halving $I$ would
cut $\sim$30--40\% if CellArea derived. Artefact; ideal $\sim$0.07--0.08\,$\mu$m$^2$.

# Ramulator 2.1 User Guide

- [1. Overview](#1-overview)
- [2. Using Ramulator 2.1](#2-using-ramulator-21)
- [3. Your First Run](#3-your-first-run)
- [4. Writing Configurations](#4-writing-configurations)
- [5. Validation and Regression Tests](#5-validation-and-regression-tests)
- [6. gem5 Integration](#6-gem5-integration)
- [7. Using Ramulator as a pure C++ Library](#7-using-ramulator-as-a-pure-c-library)
- [8. Extending Ramulator](#8-extending-ramulator)
- [9. How Ramulator Works Internally](#9-how-ramulator-works-internally)
- [10. Trace Visualizer](#10-trace-visualizer)

## 1. Overview

### 1.1 Introduction

Ramulator 2.1 is a modern, modular, and extensible cycle-level DRAM simulator. It is the successor of Ramulator 1.0 [Kim+, CAL'16] and a major overhaul of Ramulator 2.0 [Luo+, CAL'23]. The goal of Ramulator 2.1 is to enable rapid and agile implementation and evaluation of design changes in the memory controller and DRAM to meet the increasing research effort in improving the performance, security, and reliability of memory systems. Ramulator 2.1 features a clean and modular C++ codebase with automatically generated Python wrappers that enables easy and scriptable configurations and extensions. Users can focus just on the C++ code that implements modeling and simulation logic without having to worry about manually maintaining boilerplate code.

Ramulator 2.1 can either be used as a standalone simulator that takes memory traces, or be easily integrated into other simulators as a DRAM and memory controller simulation library. We currently provide gem5 wrappers that works as a drop-in component for both SE and FS mode (tested with gem5 v25.1, FS mode tested with a post-boot checkpoint).

This Github repository contains the public version of Ramulator 2.1. From time to time, we will synchronize improvements of the code framework, additional functionalities, bug fixes, etc. from our internal version. Ramulator 2.1 welcomes your contribution as well as new ideas and implementations in the memory system.

Currently, Ramulator 2.1 provides the DRAM device and memory controller models for the following standards:
- DDR3, DDR4, DDR5
- GDDR6, GDDR7
- LPDDR5, LPDDR6
- HBM1, HBM2, HBM3, HBM4

What has changed from Ramulator 2.0:
- Aggregated bug fixes
- More comprehensive support for newer DRAM & controller features
- More comprehensive sets of test and validation workflows
- Significantly improved the ease of use, configuration, and extension
- Overall code quality improvements

If you use Ramulator 2.1/2.0 in your work, please use the following citations:
```
@misc{luo2026ramulator2.1,
	title        = {{Ramulator 2.1: A Composable Memory System Simulator for Modern DRAM Systems}},
	author       = {Luo, Haocong and Bostanc{\i}, F. Nisa and Olgun, Ataberk and Makeenkova, Maria and Malik, Ziad and Akdeniz, Ipek and Mutlu, Onur},
	year         = 2026,
	howpublished = {The 3rd Tutorial on Ramulator and DRAM Bender colocated with ICS}
}
@article{luo2024ramulator2.0,
	title   = {{Ramulator 2.0: A Modern, Modular, and Extensible DRAM Simulator}},
	author  = {Luo, Haocong and Tu{\u{g}}rul, Yahya Can and Bostanc{\i}, F. Nisa and Olgun, Ataberk and Ya{\u{g}}l{\i}k{\c{c}}{\i}, A. Giray and Mutlu, Onur},
	year    = 2024,
	journal = {IEEE Computer Architecture Letters}
}
```
### 1.2 Repository Layout

- `src/`
  C++ code for main simulator implementation.
- `python/`
  Python wrappers for easy and scriptable configuration of Ramulator.
- `examples/`
  Ready-to-run example configurations and traces.
- `tests/`
  Tests and validation workflows.
- `resources/gem5_wrappers/`
  Reference wrapper code for gem5 integration.
- `visualizer/`
  Browser-based trace visualizer (Nuxt/WebGL). See [Section 10](#10-trace-visualizer).

## 2. Using Ramulator 2.1

We highly recommend to use our container (Dockerfile available at `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`) to avoid any dependency issues. The repository is also configured to be able to be one-click opened as a Dev Container with all the dependencies already installed. The easiest way to start using and developing Ramulator 2.1 is to directly create a Codespace on the GitHub page of the Ramulator 2.1 repository. If you are using Visual Studio Code, it should automatically prompt you to reopen the repository in a Dev Container after you clone and open the repo for the first time.

If you want to set up the container locally, you can do the following steps:
```bash
docker compose up -d --build --wait
docker compose exec ramulator2 bash
```
Doing so creates a container with all the dependencies, mounts the Ramulator 2.1 repository at `/workspace`, and automatically activates `ramulator2-venv` in the container bash.

If you need to configure your own environment, please refer to Section 2.3 for detailed instructions.

### 2.2 Getting Started

From the repository root:

```bash
mkdir -p build
cd build
cmake ..
make -j
cd ..
```

This default build does three useful things:

- Builds `libramulator.so` in the repository root
- Builds the Python extension module under `python/ramulator/`
- Runs the code generator so all the automatically generated code are in sync with the source code

Then run Ramulator 2.1 in standalone mode with an example configuration:

```bash
python3 examples/example_config.py
```

You should see some example statistics being printed. You can head to Section 3 directly for detailed explanations and instructions on how to use and configure Ramulator 2.1 if you do not need to build Ramulator 2.1 in your custom environment.

### 2.3 Build Requirements

**Required:**

- A C++20 compiler, such as `g++-12` or `clang++-15`
- CMake 3.14 or newer
- Python 3.10 or newer if you want the Python bindings, the CLI, or the tests

**Auto-fetched by CMake (no manual install):**

- `yaml-cpp` — YAML configuration parsing
- `fmt` — C++ print formatting
- `nanobind` — Python-C++ bindings (only when `RAMULATOR_PYTHON_BINDINGS=ON`)
- `argparse` — command-line argument parsing (vendored in `ext/`)

---
#!/usr/bin/env sh
set -eu

case "$0" in
  */*) script_path=$0 ;;
  *) script_path=$(command -v "$0") ;;
esac

root_dir=$(CDPATH= cd -P "$(dirname "$script_path")" && pwd)
build_dir=${BUILD_DIR:-"$root_dir/build"}
build_type=${BUILD_TYPE:-Release}

if [ -z "${JOBS:-}" ]; then
  if command -v nproc >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    jobs=$(nproc)
  elif command -v getconf >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    jobs=$(getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN 2>/dev/null || printf '1\n')
  else
    jobs=1
  fi
else
  jobs=$JOBS
fi

case "$jobs" in
  ''|*[!0-9]*) jobs=1 ;;
esac

if [ "$jobs" -lt 1 ]; then
  jobs=1
fi

printf 'Configuring Ramulator in %s (%s)\n' "$build_dir" "$build_type"
cmake -S "$root_dir" -B "$build_dir" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE="$build_type" "$@"

printf 'Building Ramulator with %s job(s)\n' "$jobs"
cmake --build "$build_dir" --parallel "$jobs"
```
